entries.name: Ball lightning
entries.senseHere: A rare, still-unexplained glowing sphere seen during thunderstorms, usually lasting a few seconds before vanishing with or without leaving traces. The article treats it as a real but poorly documented atmospheric phenomenon, distinct from ordinary lightning flashes, reported mostly through eyewitness accounts rather than instruments.

entries.name: François Arago
entries.background: French astronomer and physicist of the early 19th century whose 1837 book on thunder first used the term now translated as ball lightning.

entries.name: Walther Brand
entries.background: German school official who wrote the only German-language monograph on ball lightning, first published in 1923.

entries.name: Martin A. Uman
entries.background: American lightning researcher whose group used rockets trailing metal wire to deliberately trigger lightning strikes for controlled field experiments.

entries.name: Fragmented science
entries.senseHere: A description of ball lightning research as scattered across many unconnected small studies, theories, and lab experiments rather than building toward one agreed explanation.

entries.name: Prairie Meteorite Network
entries.background: A United States photographic sky-monitoring program that photographed the night sky continuously for over a decade to track meteors and fireballs.

entries.name: ALDIS
aliases: Austrian lightning detection and information system
entries.senseHere: A network of ground sensors across Austria that detects and locates individual lightning strikes, letting researchers match reported ball lightning sightings to real strokes by time and position.

entries.name: BLIDS
entries.senseHere: Germany's equivalent lightning-detection network, used in the article to confirm the strength and location of a stroke tied to a ball lightning sighting at Neuruppin.

entries.name: Cloud–ground stroke
entries.senseHere: A lightning discharge that travels between a cloud and the earth's surface, as opposed to a cloud-to-cloud discharge that stays aloft; the article tallies how often each type coincided with ball lightning sightings.

entries.name: Wilhelm von Haidinger
entries.background: 19th-century Austrian geologist and mineralogist who was a member of the Imperial Academy of Sciences in Vienna.

entries.name: Angular diameter
entries.senseHere: The apparent size of an object as seen by an observer, measured as an angle rather than an actual physical width; Haidinger used it to record how large the glowing ball looked from his window without knowing its true distance or size.

entries.name: Walther Gerlach
entries.background: German physics professor renowned for the 1922 Stern-Gerlach experiment demonstrating spin quantization in a magnetic field.

entries.name: Roger Clifton Jennison
entries.background: British radio astronomer who worked at the Jodrell Bank Observatory before becoming a professor of physical electronics.

entries.name: Georg Wilhelm Richmann
entries.background: Baltic German physicist and member of the St Petersburg Academy of Sciences who was killed in 1753 while experimenting with atmospheric electricity, an accident later mythologized as a ball lightning strike.

entries.name: Keraunoparalysis
entries.senseHere: A short-lived paralysis or numbness in a limb caused by a nearby lightning or ball lightning strike, distinguished in the article from longer-lasting nerve damage or psychological trauma from the same event.

entries.name: Jean-Martin Charcot
entries.background: French physician considered the founder of modern neurology, based at the Salpêtrière Hospital in Paris, who taught Sigmund Freud.

entries.name: Soil strike theory
aliases: Abrahamson and Dinniss soil strike theory
entries.senseHere: An explanation proposing that ball lightning forms when a lightning strike vaporizes minerals in soil, producing a glowing ball whose light comes from burning metal and silicon particles in the air.

entries.name: Slitless spectroscopy
entries.senseHere: A camera technique using a diffraction grating instead of a narrow slit to spread an object's light into a spectrum, letting researchers identify which chemical elements were glowing in a recorded ball lightning event.
